title: Who wrote this digit? Writer identification with CNNs and Siamese networks
text:
6.1 CNN
The CNN hyperparameter search varied dropout (0, 0.3, 0.5), depth (one to three convolutional layers) and learning rate (0.0003, 0.001, 0.003), one setting at a time. Interactions were not tested; runs used three seeds, one validation session, loss-based stopping (patience 5) and a 50-epoch cap. In Figure 13, three layers with dropout 0.3 and learning rate 0.001 performed best, averaging 49.9% validation accuracy. Depth had the clearest effect. Dropout results (45%, 42%, 43%) were within seed variation, while learning rate 0.003 was less stable (spread 0.052 versus about 0.025). These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the limited search design.








Figure 13: CNN validation accuracy (session 4) when one hyperparameter is changed at a time from the baseline (2 convolution layers, dropout 0.3, learning rate 0.001). Grey points are the three seeds; black points and lines are their means. Early stopping on validation loss (patience 5, at most 50 epochs).





The one-layer model and learning rate 0.0003 reached the 50-epoch cap while improving, so Figure 13 may underestimate their performance. Later runs used validation accuracy for stopping. In Figure 13, loss-based stopping selected epoch 3 for the three-layer model, stopping at epoch 8 and restoring those weights. Overconfidence increased validation loss while accuracy still improved, disadvantaging the deeper model. It nevertheless outperformed the two-layer model; Table 8 compares stopping rules.

The three-layer model performs better under both rules in Table 8, but the advantage depends on stopping. Loss-based stopping (patience 5, maximum 50 epochs) gave a 7.8-point advantage; accuracy-based stopping (patience 10, maximum 150) increased it to 11.1 points. Accuracy-based stopping avoids penalties from rising cross-entropy, while short patience can stop slow learners prematurely.

Because the three-layer model overfits, regularisation was tested. In Table 9, dropout 0.5 changed validation accuracy by only 0.1 points (about 0.1 standard errors, likely noise), but reduced the training-validation gap from 30.7 to 11.9 points and cross-entropy from 2.36 to 2.04. The smaller gap partly reflects Keras measuring training accuracy with dropout active; lower cross-entropy also suggests less overconfidence. Validation accuracy remained near 59.6%. L2 left accuracy and the gap largely unchanged but worsened cross-entropy to 2.45; combined with dropout 0.5, accuracy fell to 58.4%. The selected model therefore remains three layers, dropout 0.3 and no L2.

section: 7.1 CNN results by digit and session
text:
7.1 CNN results by digit and session

To assess session effects, the three-layer CNN was trained on three sessions, stopped on a fourth and tested on the remaining session as a “new day.” Each session served in turn as the test set. Grey points in Figure 14 show results across three seeds.
Accuracy ranged from 53.3% on session 4 to 69.5% on session 2, averaging 60.5%. This range was 7.6 times seed variation, indicating a strong session effect. The main test session, session 5, averaged 59.2% and was typical. Session 4 remained hardest despite being used for tuning, suggesting it was more difficult for the model.








Figure 14: Leave-one-session-out: test accuracy of the 3-layer CNN when each session in turn is the new day. Each model trains on three of the other sessions and early-stops on the fourth (the session before the held-out one). Grey points are three seeds; black points are their means. Holding out session 5 is the main split of Section 4.





Table 10 compares accuracy for each digit (1 000 test images) with each session’s overall accuracy. The best digit changes by session. Across all five sessions, accuracy ranges from 58% for digit 3 to 63% for digit 0, suggesting digit 0 carries more writer information on average. Yet digit 2 is best in sessions 2 and 4 and worst in session 5. Digit rankings therefore do not generalise reliably. The all-digits row repeats the session pattern in Figure 14.

In Figure 15, models predict the same session-5 test images (1 000 per digit): one is trained on all digits (15 000 images), the other on one digit only (3 000 images). Blue points show standalone information: digit 4 reaches 67% accuracy, digit 0 47%, and digits 1–3 about 53–54%. The gap from the all-digit model measures transfer from other digits. This is largest for digit 0 (+17 points), whose shape alone appears less distinctive; small gaps for digits 1–4 suggest their images often suffice. This partly agrees with Figure 7: on session 5, the all-digit model performs best on digit 0 and worst on digit 2.

title: Who wrote this digit? Writer identification with CNNs and Siamese networks
text:
7.3 Side by side
Section 4 and Section 5 each score their model the way it was trained for: the CNN as a 20-way classifier, the Siamese network as a same/different matcher. To compare them directly, R/eval_embeddings.R scores all three embedding spaces – a PCA baseline (the top 32 principal components of pixels, fitted on a training-session sample, giving the CNN and Siamese embeddings a non-learned reference point), the CNN’s 32-unit embedding layer, and the Siamese encoder’s 32-unit embedding – on the exact same data/test_pairs.csv pairs and the exact same nearest-centroid identification task (classify a session-5 test image to whichever training writer’s embedding centroid it’s closest to).

Figure 18: Matching AUC by digit (same-digit test pairs only) for the PCA baseline, CNN and Siamese network.





On overall matching, the ranking in Table 11 is CNN > Siamese > PCA: the CNN embedding reaches 0.943 AUC against the Siamese network’s 0.844 and the PCA baseline’s 0.767, with equal error rate telling the same story in reverse. That’s a little surprising given the Siamese network is the one directly trained to minimise exactly this kind of pairwise distance – the gap is explained by data/test_pairs.csv including cross-digit pairs, which the Siamese network never saw in training (it was trained on same-digit pairs only, Section 5) and matches much worse on; restricted to same-digit pairs, Figure 18 shows the Siamese network is competitive with or ahead of the CNN on most digits. Nearest-centroid identification tells a different story again: the CNN embedding reaches 58.1% accuracy, clearly ahead of the PCA baseline’s 38.9%, while the Siamese embedding trails both at 24.0% – well above the 5% chance rate, but evidently the Siamese network’s contrastive training pulls same-writer pairs together locally without necessarily arranging all 20 writers into compact, well-separated global clusters the way a 20-class softmax classifier is directly pushed to.
That split points to which model suits which question. If the task is “which of these 20 known writers wrote this”, the CNN is the right tool and the cheaper one to run at inference (one forward pass, one softmax); if it ever needs to cover a 21st writer, though, it needs retraining from scratch, because the output layer itself is sized to 20 classes. If the task is “did the same person write these two samples” – including for someone never seen in training – the Siamese network is the right tool, exactly because it was designed and evaluated for that (Section 5’s unseen-writer experiment); its cost is a less interpretable per-writer signal, as the centroid result above shows.
The digit rankings mostly agree across methods: digit 0 is at or near the best-matching digit for both the CNN and the Siamese network in Figure 18, broadly consistent with the EDA’s digit-0-restricted PCA (Figure 5) showing clean writer clusters for that digit. The session gap – how much farther apart same-writer pairs sit when they come from different sessions rather than the same one – is present for every model: cross-session distances exceed same-session distances by a factor of 5.9x for the PCA baseline, 3.6x for the CNN, and 2.8x for the Siamese network, confirming that the session drift documented in Section 2 costs every model some matching accuracy, not just the simplest one.
As with Section 3, these numbers should be read with the data’s limits in mind: 20 simulated writers is a small, closed, easy world next to real-world identification, and all three embedding spaces are evaluated on one simulated test session (session 5) – a real deployment spanning many more sessions, writers and genuinely different pens and paper would likely show a larger gap between methods, and a larger session effect, than measured here.
